Summary:
Hannes Strydom's time has come. He has been breaking the law, threatening staff and feeding the black market codeine market for years. He's pointed fingers at allegedly dishonest thieving employees - always claiming innocence through convenient so-called ignorance.

BUT he's crossed too many people and they have united in their shared dislike of the man they once respected and have helped us collect evidence to expose the dodgy dealings once and for all.

We've got documents, we've got insider interviews, we've got internal stock ledgers, we've got undercover footage. And if all goes well, we'll have an pharmacy council inspection and on-camera confront.


Further information:
SETTING THE SCENE
What is Codeine?
Codeine is considered a mild painkiller , classified as a “weak opioid” – 10mg of codeine is equal to 1mg of oral morphine. When taking opioid-based drugs, your brain releases feel-good chemicals and it doesn’t take too much to get to a drowsy, pleasurable high. These euphoriant effects, often reinforce continued use - codeine, therefore, poses a risk of developing tolerance and eventually dependence.

Codeine is an internationally controlled substance in terms of the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotics, and its use is monitored by the International Narcotics Control Board.

GLOBALLY
At least 25 countries, including Germany, Japan, Australia, the US and Nigeria have banned over-the-counter codeine sales. A (2013-2019) study of 31 countries ranked SA highest when it came to how much over-the-counter codeine is sold in the form of painkillers or cough syrup.

CODEINE REGULATIONS IN SA
Codeine-containing cough syrups are regulated in terms of Schedule 2 and Schedule 3 to the Medicines Act. Unless prescribed by an authorised prescriber, these products can only be sold by a registered pharmacist, or a post-basic pharmacist’s assistant under the personal supervision of a pharmacist, at a licenced pharmacy. The sale of a Schedule 2 product has to be documented by the dispensing pharmacist by capturing the patient’s identity and address. In theory, this should allow for repeat purchasing to be detected - However, it doesn’t stop patients from visiting multiple pharmacies or seeing multiple prescribers, nor does it address criminal activity.

WHAT’s THE ISSUE
There are two sides to the problem of codeine abuse or addiction. The first is the inappropriate sale of codeine-containing medicines by pharmacists or inappropriate prescription by authorised prescribers. The second is codeine-containing substances being diverted into unregulated distribution channels through theft or illegal sale by “unscrupulous practitioners”

ANDY GRAY - a Senior Lecturer in the Division of Pharmacology, Discipline of Pharmaceutical Sciences, School of Health Sciences, UKZN
“There is evidence of large quantities of codeine-containing cough mixtures being sold in markets, from retail outlets such as hairdressers, and also moved across borders into neighbouring states. The origin of those diverted stocks has not been identified,” he says. “There is also evidence that some pharmacies and dispensing practices are procuring large volumes from wholesalers. None have yet been prosecuted.”

OUR STORY
The Pharma-Valu chain of 10 pharmacies are owned by former Springbok Hannes Strydom. He also owns a Wholesale Pharmacy called Traders.

Since February this year, this investigation has uncovered a string of illegal transactions at this Pharmacy Group. But the dodgy dealings have been going on for years. Hannes Strydom is going to blame a former employee – but they worked together and were best buds until they fell out. And sadly for Strydom – we have proof that the dodgy deals continued after his side-kick left.

ALSO – we are hoping to have the side-kick on camera.

Unless prescribed by an authorised prescriber, these products can only be sold by a registered pharmacist, or a post-basic pharmacist’s assistant under the personal supervision of a pharmacist, at a licenced pharmacy. The sale of a Schedule 2 product has to be documented by the dispensing pharmacist by capturing the patient’s identity and address. metadata.Further information: SETTING THE SCENE What is Codeine? Codeine is considered a mild painkiller , classified as a “weak opioid” – 10mg of codeine is equal to 1mg of oral morphine. When taking opioid-based drugs, your brain releases feel-good chemicals and it doesn’t take too much to get to a drowsy, pleasurable high. These euphoriant effects, often reinforce continued use - codeine, therefore, poses a risk of developing tolerance and eventually dependence. Codeine is an internationally controlled substance in terms of the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotics, and its use is monitored by the International Narcotics Control Board. GLOBALLY At least 25 countries, including Germany, Japan, Australia, the US and Nigeria have banned over-the-counter codeine sales. A (2013-2019) study of 31 countries ranked SA highest when it came to how much over-the-counter codeine is sold in the form of painkillers or cough syrup. CODEINE REGULATIONS IN SA Codeine-containing cough syrups are regulated in terms of Schedule 2 and Schedule 3 to the Medicines Act. Unless prescribed by an authorised prescriber, these products can only be sold by a registered pharmacist, or a post-basic pharmacist’s assistant under the personal supervision of a pharmacist, at a licenced pharmacy. The sale of a Schedule 2 product has to be documented by the dispensing pharmacist by capturing the patient’s identity and address. In theory, this should allow for repeat purchasing to be detected - However, it doesn’t stop patients from visiting multiple pharmacies or seeing multiple prescribers, nor does it address criminal activity. WHAT’s THE ISSUE There are two sides to the problem of codeine abuse or addiction. The first is the inappropriate sale of codeine-containing medicines by pharmacists or inappropriate prescription by authorised prescribers. The second is codeine-containing substances being diverted into unregulated distribution channels through theft or illegal sale by “unscrupulous practitioners” ANDY GRAY - a Senior Lecturer in the Division of Pharmacology, Discipline of Pharmaceutical Sciences, School of Health Sciences, UKZN “There is evidence of large quantities of codeine-containing cough mixtures being sold in markets, from retail outlets such as hairdressers, and also moved across borders into neighbouring states. The origin of those diverted stocks has not been identified,” he says. “There is also evidence that some pharmacies and dispensing practices are procuring large volumes from wholesalers.
